title: Deep Cylindrical Vessel (Fukabachi)
medium: Earthenware with cord-marked decoration and sculptural rim

altText: A tall, deep clay pot with an elaborate, sculpted rim. Its brown surface is covered in pressed, cord-like patterns and ridges.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, creditLine, classification, tags, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A large earthenware vessel made in Japan during the Middle Jōmon period, about 3500 to 2500 BCE. Its surface is decorated with cord markings and its rim is shaped like sculpture. The name Jōmon means cord-marked, after the patterns on this kind of pottery.

descriptions.k: This is a very, very old clay pot. It is tall and deep. The top edge is fancy and sculpted, almost like a crown. The sides have patterns pressed into them. People made it by hand in Japan thousands of years ago.
descriptions.g12: People in Japan made this clay pot by hand more than four thousand years ago. It is tall and deep. The top edge is shaped like sculpture. The sides have pressed patterns made with cord. Why do you think someone took the time to decorate a pot?
descriptions.g35: This pot comes from the Jōmon culture of Japan, one of the oldest pottery traditions in the world. Jōmon means cord-marked, because makers pressed cord into the wet clay to make patterns. The rim rises into a sculpted shape. Potters had no wheel, so they built vessels by hand. Why might they have made a tall pot so decorative? What could it have been used for?
descriptions.g68: Made around 3500 to 2500 BCE, this deep vessel shows that early Jōmon-culture potters cared about form as well as function. The name Jōmon, meaning cord-marked, comes from the patterned surfaces. Pots like this were built by hand without a wheel and fired at fairly low temperatures. The sculptural rim is the most dramatic part. Archaeologists debate how such vessels were used, so look closely: what evidence suggests cooking, storage, ceremony, or all three?
descriptions.g910: This Middle Jōmon vessel combines utility with striking sculptural design. Its deep, cylindrical body is textured with cord-marked decoration, while the rim develops into an elaborate crest. Scholars generally see Jōmon pottery as evidence of settled or semi-settled hunter-gatherer communities with a strong decorative tradition, though how specific vessels were used is debated. Consider how the contrast between the repeating surface pattern and the irregular rim directs the eye upward and gives the pot presence.
descriptions.g1112: Jōmon pottery challenges older assumptions that ceramic traditions arise only with farming: these makers were largely hunter-gatherers. This deep vessel's cord-marked body and sculptural rim reveal sustained investment in form and decoration. Interpretations vary about whether elaborate examples served everyday cooking, storage, ritual, or display, and the surviving evidence is incomplete. The modern label art also reflects later collecting and museum frameworks rather than the makers' own categories. How should we weigh visual evidence against such uncertainty?

teacherNote.context: Middle Jōmon pottery from Japan, ca. 3500 to 2500 BCE. The Jōmon tradition is among the earliest pottery traditions known, made by largely hunter-gatherer communities.
directions: Let students press string and rope into modeling clay to see how cord-marked patterns form.
Ask groups to propose and defend three possible uses for the vessel, using visible evidence.
Discuss how archaeologists decide what an object was for when no written record survives.
